title: Todd Packer

jokes.text: Dwight explains he has the best-stocked survival shelter in northeastern Pennsylvania and must eat everything before it expires.
jokes.setup: Dwight opens with a serious, authoritative declaration about his survival shelter
jokes.punchline: The mundane problem is that he has to eat eight-year-old canned goods before they expire — treating apocalypse prep like a meal-planning inconvenience
jokes.explanation: Pure Dwight character comedy — the absurd logic of prepper life rendered as a mundane meal-planning problem. Strong character integration; only Dwight would frame eating expired canned goods as a lifestyle convenience.

jokes.text: Jim offers cheese from his fridge; Dwight counters 'I've got some cheese you might like too. In between my toes.'
jokes.setup: Jim makes a mundane, friendly offer about cheese to mock Dwight's expired food
jokes.punchline: Dwight one-ups with disgusting toe-cheese, delivered completely straight
jokes.explanation: Functional gross-out gag. Dwight's obliviousness to social norms sells it, but it's a fairly predictable escalation of the cheese conversation into disgusting territory.

jokes.text: Dwight's apocalypse monologue: 'Kevin will be eaten. Pam will be taken slave. Jim will be made a warlord's jester. Meredith will do okay.'
jokes.setup: Dwight launches into a dramatic post-apocalyptic scenario where everyone will suffer
jokes.punchline: 'Meredith will do okay' — the casual, almost admiring exception for the office's most feral member lands as a perfect character-specific punchline
jokes.explanation: Exceptional piece of character comedy. The list format builds a comedic rhythm (eaten, enslaved, jesters) and then the deadpan 'Meredith will do okay' is a perfect subversion — it says everything about both Dwight's worldview and Meredith's chaotic survivability without a single wasted word. Highly quotable. This is the kind of joke that rewards rewatches because it deepens your appreciation of Meredith as a character.

jokes.text: Packer's talking head: 'I got a couple love bumps on my ding-dong, so I was like, Game over.'
jokes.setup: Packer explains he thought he was becoming too much of a womanizer
jokes.punchline: The reason he stopped wasn't growth or maturity — it was STI symptoms, delivered in juvenile slang with zero shame
jokes.explanation: Works as character establishment for Packer — it immediately tells you everything about him. The phrase 'love bumps on my ding-dong' is memorably juvenile, which is the point. Somewhat low-brow but earns it through character specificity.

jokes.text: 'It was the best of times. It was the awesomest of times.'
jokes.setup: Packer builds on the 'best of times' Dickens allusion
jokes.punchline: 'Awesomest' — mangling a literary reference by going bigger and dumber instead of the expected parallel structure
jokes.explanation: Quick, efficient joke that reveals Packer's half-educated bravado. He knows enough to invoke Dickens but replaces the payoff with the dumbest possible word. Good economy.

jokes.text: Packer to Holly: 'Michael, I thought we were meeting Holly today, not Jennifer Aniston.'
jokes.setup: Packer meets Holly for the first time in a professional HR context
jokes.punchline: He immediately deploys a cheesy celebrity-comparison compliment, which is both sycophantic and undermining to Michael simultaneously
jokes.explanation: Standard Packer schmooze — functional but not particularly sharp. The Jennifer Aniston reference is dated even in-universe and feels like easy flattery humor rather than genuinely crafted comedy.

jokes.text: Michael tells Holly that Packer is funniest after five shots and it also helps if she's had five shots. Holly: 'I already have.'
jokes.setup: Michael awkwardly coaches Holly on how to handle Packer's interview, suggesting shots help
jokes.punchline: Holly reveals she's already pre-gamed the Packer interview — simultaneously funny and a little sad
jokes.explanation: Tight two-beat joke with a great callback structure. Holly's deadpan 'I already have' is perfectly economical and says a lot about how seriously she's taking this interview. Works both as comedy and mild character revelation. The rewatch bonus: knowing Holly's character makes this even funnier on repeat viewings.

jokes.text: Michael introduces Packer: 'a man who needs no introduction, probably because most of you have done it with him. Just kidding. He wouldn't be interested in any of you.'
jokes.setup: Michael builds the classic 'needs no introduction' setup for Packer
jokes.punchline: Double subversion: the sexual implication followed immediately by the insult that Packer has standards too low/high to apply to this office
jokes.explanation: Michael trying to do Packer-style humor and landing a double-edged joke that accidentally insults everyone. The structure is good — the correction makes it funnier than just the first punchline. Character-specific: Michael thinks he's being cool and inclusive while actually burning everyone.

jokes.text: Packer: 'It's great to be among friends. And until then, you suckers will do.'
jokes.setup: Packer appears to begin a warm greeting to the office
jokes.punchline: Hard pivot — he doesn't consider any of them friends and says so immediately
jokes.explanation: Efficient and mean. Good economy — the setup and pivot are compressed into a single breath. Packer's complete shamelessness in saying the quiet part loud is his defining character trait, and this moment establishes it cleanly for the ensemble.

jokes.text: Michael: 'He is turning in his condoms for a condominium, although he's probably going to have to use condoms from here on out.'
jokes.setup: Michael does a series of 'turning in X for Y' transitions for Packer's career change
jokes.punchline: The condom/condominium wordplay followed by the implication that Packer's STI situation now requires condoms — a callback to Packer's own talking head
jokes.explanation: A two-layer joke: the wordplay is functional (condoms/condominium), and the callback to Packer's STI admission makes it unexpectedly sharp. Michael probably thinks he's being clever and funny without fully registering what he's implying. The awkward laugh-then-silence structure this would create in a room is good comedy.

jokes.text: Holly's visible discomfort and confused reaction as Michael praises Packer's hiring in front of the whole staff
jokes.setup: Holly approved Packer's transfer based on Michael's recommendation, now watching Packer be instantly offensive to the entire office
jokes.punchline: Her 'Yes, I did' response to incredulous coworkers registers as instant regret — a silent acknowledgment that she may have made a mistake
jokes.explanation: A functional cringe beat. Holly's defensiveness ('What don't you understand about the word approved?') shifts to comedy when you realize she's also processing buyer's remorse. The joke is partly visual — her demeanor in this scene telling the story.

jokes.text: Gabe fell in the shower and it took the fire department forever to get there.
jokes.setup: Gabe and Erin arrive late to the meeting
jokes.punchline: The reason is that Gabe fell in the shower and required fire department extraction — his physical helplessness is the joke
jokes.explanation: Quick sight gag/character beat about Gabe's pathetic physical frailty. The comedy comes from the extreme consequence (fire department) for something mundane (shower fall). Lands better if you already find Gabe comedically helpless.

jokes.text: Packer brags that the old reception computer's IP address was 'one.'
jokes.setup: Packer justifies getting Erin a new computer by insulting the old one
jokes.punchline: IP number was one — a technologically absurd insult that works because it's almost plausible while being completely wrong, and delivered with total confidence
jokes.explanation: Clever tech-joke that's funny on two levels: for people who know IP addressing (it's wrong but sounds almost right) and for people who don't (it's clearly an insult meaning 'very old'). The specificity of 'one' is what makes it work — a vague 'really old number' would be half as funny.

jokes.text: Jim's talking head: he cleaned up their daughter at 4am, implying that qualifies as 'helping someone out' and therefore feeling good
jokes.setup: Pam says she helped someone and it feels good
jokes.punchline: Jim's passive-aggressive 'So you know the feeling' after noting he was up at 4am cleaning their baby — parenting as competitive martyrdom
jokes.explanation: Relatable new-parent humor delivered with The Office's signature understatement. The joke works because Jim's deadpan keeps it from becoming too sitcom-sappy. A small but effective character moment.

jokes.text: Michael asking Dwight to permanently relocate so Packer can have his desk, and revealing Packer had carved 'Packer was here and so was your mom' under the desk years prior
jokes.setup: Michael asks Dwight to give up his desk of 10 years as if it's a small favor; Dwight says his name is carved under the desk
jokes.punchline: The carving is 'Packer was here and so was your mom' — a childish 'your mom' burn that Dwight has been sitting on top of for years without knowing
jokes.explanation: A well-planted visual gag — the image of Packer carving a 'your mom' joke under Dwight's desk at some point in the past is delightfully specific and immature. Dwight's reaction (demanding to see it, then being confronted with it) adds a cringe layer. The reveal structure is clean.

jokes.text: Packer to the Zen garden: 'What are you growing in here, bull crap?'
jokes.setup: Packer encounters the office's Zen garden
jokes.punchline: He immediately insults it in the crudest possible terms, unable to process office culture
jokes.explanation: Functional Packer-being-a-Neanderthal joke. Not particularly inspired but moves quickly. The Zen garden detail is a nice specificity for the joke.

jokes.text: Oscar and the others to Holly: 'Don't what's up us. You think you're so cute with your pretty blond hair. Pull it back.'
jokes.setup: Holly casually greets the group who are furious about Packer's hiring
jokes.punchline: Oscar (and presumably others) redirect their Packer frustration into petty, hilariously personal complaints about Holly's hair
jokes.explanation: The escalation from HR grievance to 'pull your hair back' is a great swerve — the specificity of the hair complaint is unexpected and funny. Oscar leading this charge is perfect character casting.

jokes.text: Phyllis: 'That's how he gets you to take off your panties.' Then Holly: 'Why are you nodding?' Pam: 'United front.'
jokes.setup: Holly defends Packer for being 'nothing but nice' to her
jokes.punchline: Phyllis's crude explanation that niceness is Packer's seduction strategy; Pam silently nodding in agreement, then explaining 'United front' when caught
jokes.explanation: A triple-layer joke: Phyllis's crude but perceptive observation, Holly's incredulous 'Why are you nodding?', and Pam's deadpan 'United front.' The rhythm is excellent and each beat escalates the comedy. 'United front' is particularly quotable — it perfectly captures Office workplace solidarity absurdity.

jokes.text: Oscar: 'We can't fire someone because we don't like him. Right. This isn't the U.S. government.' Holly: 'What are you referencing?' Oscar: 'Everything.'
jokes.setup: Holly says they can't fire someone just because they don't like him
jokes.punchline: Oscar's political non-sequitur followed by the perfectly dismissive 'Everything' when asked to clarify
jokes.explanation: Oscar's vague but comprehensive political cynicism is perfectly in character — he's the 'smart one' who gestures at broader cultural critique. 'Everything' as the answer to 'what are you referencing' is extremely economical and funny. A quick joke that lands cleanly.

jokes.text: Kelly: 'He humped Michael.' Holly: 'Well, if that's the case, I guess I've got to be fired, too.'
jokes.setup: Holly asks if anyone has concrete complaints about Packer; Kelly mentions that Packer humped Michael
jokes.punchline: Holly's self-incriminating joke — implying she has also been intimate with Michael — played deadpan
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. Holly's deadpan self-inclusion ('I guess I've got to be fired too') is a perfectly timed, character-specific response that simultaneously acknowledges her relationship with Michael, defuses the situation, and gets a huge laugh. It's the kind of line that makes you appreciate the character's wit. High quotability.

jokes.text: The Yarmouth Regatta sailing video enthusiast ('Luff him up! Luff him up!') watching their video on the new computer Packer gave Erin
jokes.setup: Someone is excitedly watching a sailing regatta video
jokes.punchline: The sudden, specific sailing jargon ('Luff him up!') in an office setting is an absurd background detail
jokes.explanation: A quirky background character detail that's more of a texture joke. The specificity of 'Luff him up!' is funny for sailing-literate viewers, but it's a minor grace note rather than a constructed joke.

jokes.text: Packer: 'Gwen Stefani has this computer.' Then to Pam: 'What does a guy have to do to whom to get one of them?'
jokes.setup: Packer admires Erin's new computer and wants one
jokes.punchline: 'What does a guy have to do to whom' — grammatically broken innuendo that reveals Packer's cognitive approach to everything through a sexual lens without even managing to complete the implication properly
jokes.explanation: The broken grammar ('to whom') is the unexpected comic element — Packer starts a sentence he doesn't know how to finish, and the result is funnier than if he'd completed the innuendo. 'Gwen Stefani has this computer' is also a great character detail — his celebrity reference points are revealing.

jokes.text: Andy: 'If you donated my computer to Africa, it would become famous as the slowest computer in Africa.'
jokes.setup: Andy argues his computer is bad and he deserves a new one
jokes.punchline: The hyperbolic specificity — not just slow, but famous for being slow in Africa — escalates the complaint to absurdity
jokes.explanation: A very quotable, well-structured hyperbole joke. The 'famous as the slowest' escalation is tight and the geographic specificity sells it. This is the kind of throwaway line that sticks with you.

jokes.text: Stanley's non-reaction to being mentioned; Pam: 'So something good happening to Stanley is crazy now?' — Stanley says nothing
jokes.setup: Pam says if she gets Andy a computer she'd have to get one for everyone, including Stanley
jokes.punchline: Pam's defensive 'So something good happening to Stanley is crazy now?' — and Stanley's complete non-involvement in advocating for himself
jokes.explanation: A quick Stanley joke that works because of his consistent character — he's so checked-out he doesn't even advocate for himself. The joke is really Pam being indignant on behalf of someone who isn't indignant at all.

jokes.text: Phyllis: 'What, are you gonna play mahjongg faster?' to Andy's computer argument
jokes.setup: Andy argues he needs a faster computer for work
jokes.punchline: Phyllis implying that Andy's actual computer use is mahjongg, which would be unaffected by speed
jokes.explanation: Very economical line — maximum information per word. Phyllis simultaneously burns Andy, implies the computers are only used for games anyway, and stays perfectly in character as the sardonic background employee. 'Mahjongg' is the perfect game to name.

jokes.text: Packer: 'Three muske-queers.' Kelly: 'Mean, but good.'
jokes.setup: Packer enters to find Ryan, Kelly, and someone else together
jokes.punchline: A homophobic portmanteau that's immediately undermined by Kelly's reaction — 'Mean, but good' — which reveals how confused people are about whether to enjoy Packer
jokes.explanation: The actual insult is lowbrow, but Kelly's 'Mean, but good' reaction is the real joke — it exposes how Packer's cruelty confuses and half-disarms people who know they shouldn't laugh. Kelly's response is sharper than the setup.

jokes.text: 'Mean, but good.' — office character's reaction to Packer's 'muske-queers' joke
jokes.setup: Packer delivers his homophobic pun
jokes.punchline: Someone immediately summarizes the joke's moral status as 'Mean, but good' — inadvertently describing how The Office itself navigates Packer's humor
jokes.explanation: This three-word meta-commentary is sharper than the joke it reacts to. 'Mean, but good' is The Office articulating its own comedic philosophy about Packer through a character's mouth — the show is acknowledging that Packer's humor is objectionable yet effective, which is exactly the tension the episode is exploring. High economy (9.0) and a genuine rewatch bonus for meta-awareness.

jokes.text: Packer to Todd (Stanley?): 'She's turned into a bitch. Most days she's great, but some days she acts like her mom.'
jokes.setup: Packer is asked about connecting with his daughter now that he's off the road
jokes.punchline: He calls his daughter a bitch in public, then softens it by specifying it's only on her 'mom days'
jokes.explanation: Packer being unselfconsciously terrible about his family. The attempted softening ('most days she's great') is actually what makes it worse and funnier. Works as character establishment but not exceptional writing.

jokes.text: Packer to Kevin: 'Since when did you learn how to read?' Kevin: 'I do know how to read, though.' Packer: 'Yeah. You know how to read a menu.'
jokes.setup: Someone tells Packer he should write a book; Packer turns it on Kevin
jokes.punchline: Kevin's defensive 'I do know how to read' followed by Packer's escalation — 'yeah, a menu' — which is a specific, cruel, and accurate insult
jokes.explanation: Three-beat structure with a clean escalation. Kevin's sincere self-defense ('I do know how to read, though') is the real comedy — his earnestness makes Packer's 'a menu' hit harder. The insult is specific enough to be funny while being clearly mean.

jokes.text: Kevin's talking head: 'I... He's right. I mean, I could lose some weight.'
jokes.setup: Kevin has just been insulted about his reading ability and weight
jokes.punchline: Kevin's confessional registers only the weight comment — not even addressing the literacy insult — and agrees with it, missing the point entirely
jokes.explanation: A perfect Kevin moment. The confession format magnifies his obliviousness — he agrees with the insult but only partially engages with it, and the half-start 'I...' before he corrects course is beautifully scripted hesitation. The fact that he doesn't even address the reading jab is the real joke. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Dwight's talking head: 'Kevin, in sumo culture, you would be considered a promising up-and-comer.'
jokes.setup: Following the Packer/Kevin weight exchange
jokes.punchline: Dwight's earnest attempt to comfort Kevin by framing his body type as an asset in a specific cultural context — completely straight-faced and oddly specific
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. 'Promising up-and-comer' applied to sumo culture is both a specific comfort and an accidental insult — Dwight is genuinely trying to help, and his reference point is sumo wrestling. The word 'promising' implies Kevin still has growing to do, which makes it doubly funny. Only Dwight could deliver this line. The economy is exceptional — 15 words that do enormous character work. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Erin gave Packer the computer meant for reception because 'he seemed to really need a new computer and he knows so much about that one'
jokes.setup: Pam discovers that Erin has given away the new computer to Packer
jokes.punchline: Erin's completely earnest justification — she was charmed by Packer into giving away company property — and her naive logic ('he knows so much about that one')
jokes.explanation: A good Erin character joke — her guilelessness makes her the perfect Packer victim. The joke works because we can see exactly how Packer manipulated her and Erin genuinely sees no problem.

jokes.text: Pam coaching Andy to 'take three deep breaths' while clearly trying to manage her own frustration about the computer situation
jokes.setup: Andy is frustrated; Pam offers breathing advice
jokes.punchline: 'I'm not freaking out.' Pam is obviously freaking out; giving stress advice while stressed is the irony
jokes.explanation: A functional irony beat but fairly standard. The 'I'm not freaking out' denial while visibly freaking out is a well-worn comedy structure.

jokes.text: Michael to Dwight as he sends him on an errand: 'Please make sure nobody is humping me.' Then asks him to take Dwight's ant farm to the annex.
jokes.setup: Michael is sending Dwight to the annex
jokes.punchline: Michael's bizarre non-sequitur request to 'make sure nobody is humping me' — delivered as if it's a standard office request
jokes.explanation: An odd Michael moment that works mainly because it's so unexpected in the middle of a mundane task assignment. The ant farm detail layered on top is a nice absurdist touch.

jokes.text: 'I think the ants are waking up. They need to start farming soon.'
jokes.setup: Dwight asks someone going back to the annex to deliver something
jokes.punchline: Dwight is maintaining an ant farm in the office and is worried about their agricultural schedule — delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Dwight's ant farm agricultural concerns are pure character comedy — the specificity of 'start farming soon' implies Dwight has a monitored ant farming schedule. Only Dwight would treat an ant farm with the same urgency as actual farm management. High character integration.

jokes.text: Dwight asking if he should get 'stripes shaved into the side of his head.' Michael: 'Did Todd tell you to do that?' Dwight: 'Yes.'
jokes.setup: Dwight casually asks if he should get a haircut modification
jokes.punchline: Michael immediately knows Packer put him up to it; Dwight's simple 'yes' confirms he was manipulated without any self-awareness
jokes.explanation: A great small beat about Dwight's surprising susceptibility to a certain type of confident male authority. The economy is excellent — the whole joke lands in three words ('Did Todd?' / 'Yes.'). Dwight wanting to please someone he finds impressive is a revealing character moment.

jokes.text: Holly: 'He's not funny at all.' Michael: 'So I'm less funny than not funny at all?'
jokes.setup: Holly tries to reassure Michael that he's funnier than Packer by saying Packer isn't funny
jokes.punchline: Michael's logical trap — if Packer isn't funny, and Michael is less funny than Packer, where does that leave Michael?
jokes.explanation: Sharp logical comedy — Michael accidentally constructs a valid syllogism that proves he's less than not-funny. The structure is tight and the character integration is strong: Michael's insecurity about being funnier than Packer accidentally leads him to undermine himself. Holly walking into it despite trying to help is the cringe layer.

jokes.text: Michael's comedy hierarchy: 'Bill Cosby, Steve Martin, Charlie Bit My Finger, Michael Scott, then all the way down here, Todd Packer.'
jokes.setup: Michael is defending his comedic status relative to Packer
jokes.punchline: Michael places himself 4th in an all-time comedy hierarchy, between 'Charlie Bit My Finger' (a YouTube video) and Todd Packer — the placement of a viral video above himself being the unintentional self-own
jokes.explanation: Episode highlight. The joke is multi-layered: (1) Michael's self-aggrandizement in placing himself on an all-time comedy list, (2) his mixed reference points (Cosby, Steve Martin, then a YouTube video of a baby), (3) the unintentional self-own of ranking a baby biting a finger above himself, and (4) the condescending placement of Packer at the bottom. The 'Charlie Bit My Finger' choice is perfectly calibrated — it's dated enough to feel like Michael's cultural touchstone, absurd enough to be funny, and the escalation from legendary stand-ups to viral video content is the core joke. Highly quotable. Only Michael Scott could earnestly construct this hierarchy.

jokes.text: Packer to Jim and Pam: 'How's the sex?'
jokes.setup: Packer encounters Jim and Pam and acknowledges they're married
jokes.punchline: Immediately asks about their sex life as a congratulatory follow-up
jokes.explanation: A quick cringe moment. Functional Packer character beat but not particularly inventive — it's exactly what you'd expect from him. The joke is almost entirely in the delivery and Jim's reaction.

jokes.text: Packer declines the hot chocolate: 'The only hot chocolate I'm into is Vivica A. Fox.'
jokes.setup: Dwight offers Packer hot chocolate; Packer declines
jokes.punchline: Packer's racist-coded response invokes a Black actress using 'hot chocolate' as a racial epithet, delivered as a 'joke'
jokes.explanation: This is deliberately the worst kind of Packer joke — racist-coded, gratuitous, and not remotely clever. The craft is low by design: the show is depicting how unfunny and offensive Packer actually is. Below-4 craft justified because the 'joke' is just a racist implication with no wit. The character integration keeps it above 3 only because it's so perfectly on-brand for Packer-as-villain.

jokes.text: Dwight offering Packer poisoned hot chocolate; Packer: 'The only hot chocolate I'm into is Vivica A. Fox.'
jokes.setup: Dwight brings Packer hot chocolate to 'let bygones be bygones'
jokes.punchline: Packer refuses and delivers a racially charged celebrity non-sequitur as his reason
jokes.explanation: The Vivica A. Fox non-sequitur is classic Packer — inappropriately specific and offensive. Works more as character texture than a well-crafted joke. The setup (Dwight's laxative scheme) is funnier than the punchline.

jokes.text: Jim intervenes in Dwight's laxative scheme: 'You know you can't actually poison him. Right?' Dwight: 'It isn't poison. It's a laxative. People take laxatives all the time. This is just a lot more of a laxative.'
jokes.setup: Jim catches Dwight preparing to poison Packer's hot chocolate
jokes.punchline: Dwight's perfectly lawyerly distinction — it's not poison, it's just 'a lot more of a laxative' — delivered with complete seriousness
jokes.explanation: Excellent character comedy. Dwight's logic is internally consistent and legally specific — he's not poisoning anyone, he's medicating them heavily without consent, which is somehow worse. The escalating self-justification ('people take laxatives all the time / this is just a lot more') is textbook Dwight rationalization. Only Dwight would make this distinction. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Jim suggests: 'Pepto-Bismol in his hot chocolate.' Dwight: 'You have got to stop with the hot chocolate stuff.'
jokes.setup: Jim and Dwight are brainstorming how to torment Packer; Jim offers a prank idea
jokes.punchline: Dwight — who just proposed a laxative overdose — shuts down Jim's far milder Pepto-Bismol idea as if Jim is the one being unreasonable
jokes.explanation: A perfect irony beat. Dwight was just planning a laxative overdose, and now he's lecturing Jim about escalating with digestive medicine — completely missing the irony of his own position. The callback structure makes it work; it rewards having paid attention to the previous joke. Strong character integration: only Dwight has this calibrated sense of what counts as 'too far.'

jokes.text: Dwight's prank idea: 'Jam his drawers so they only come out two inches. That way you can see everything in them, but you can't get at it.' Jim: 'Does Edgar Allan Poe know about that one? So sinister.'
jokes.setup: Dwight pitches his best prank idea to torment Packer
jokes.punchline: The prank is absurdly mild and inconvenient rather than genuinely evil; Jim's 'Does Edgar Allan Poe know about that one?' satirizes how seriously Dwight takes his non-threatening schemes
jokes.explanation: Dwight's obliviousness to the mildness of his 'sinister' plan is delightful, and Jim's Edgar Allan Poe reference is a perfectly calibrated mock-Gothic overreaction. The line 'you can see everything but you can't get at it' is somehow more disturbing than it should be for a drawer joke, which makes the Poe reference funnier.

jokes.text: Jim's Justin Bieber prank idea; Dwight: 'Who is Justice Beaver?' Jim: 'He's a crime-fighting beaver.'
jokes.setup: Jim suggests a prank involving Justin Bieber's name to mess with Packer
jokes.punchline: Dwight mishears 'Justin Bieber' as 'Justice Beaver' and asks who that is; Jim — completely deadpan — explains 'he's a crime-fighting beaver'
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and one of the great Jim/Dwight moments. The structure is perfect: Dwight's mishearing ('Justice Beaver') is already funny, but Jim's absolute deadpan commitment to the bit — 'He's a crime-fighting beaver' — elevates it to exceptional. It's a completely absurd improvised explanation delivered with total confidence, and the image of Jim just deciding that's the answer and moving on is priceless. This is the highest-scoring joke for structure, economy, and character integration simultaneously. Dwight will absolutely not look this up. Jim will never explain. The implication that Dwight now believes there is a crime-fighting beaver named Justice Beaver is the rewatch bonus. Culturally dated but perfect in execution.

jokes.text: Jim suggests Dwight write his top 40 prank ideas. Dwight: 'I'll email you 100.' Jim: 'Write up your list of 100, edit it down to your top 40, and I'll read it over.'
jokes.setup: Jim and Dwight are conspiring; Jim asks for a list of 40 ideas
jokes.punchline: Dwight overcommits to 100; Jim immediately commits him to writing 100 AND editing them down — knowing he'll do it
jokes.explanation: A good small character beat — Jim weaponizing Dwight's eagerness to create more work for him. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Jim books a conference room with a sign-up sheet with 'mods' (5-minute increments) to have a private conversation with Pam
jokes.setup: Jim says he wants to talk to Pam privately; Pam says 'I don't know if there's really a private place in this office'
jokes.punchline: Jim reveals he's already put up a sign-up sheet in the conference room dividing time into 5-minute 'mods,' signed them up, and it started two minutes ago
jokes.explanation: The joke is in Jim's premeditation — he anticipated Pam's objection and already solved it before she raised it. The detail of 'it started two minutes ago' adds urgency and reveals Jim was planning this entire time. Typical Jim efficiency, competently executed.

jokes.text: Dwight's drawer-jamming prank backfires immediately; the drawer jams and he can't access his own pen — 'Damn it.'
jokes.setup: Jim suggested jamming drawers; it's implied Dwight tested it on himself
jokes.punchline: Dwight immediately becomes the victim of his own prank — 'Just when we were getting going'
jokes.explanation: Perfect comeuppance comedy. The joke is efficient: we inferred Dwight would test his own prank, and the immediate payoff ('Damn it') confirms it. 'Just when we were getting going' implies Jim is also enjoying this, which adds a layer. The callback to Dwight's own idea immediately undermining him is structurally satisfying.

jokes.text: Dwight's 400 prank ideas: 'Number three, eat a frog.' 'Number four, eat a dog.' 'One thirty-five? Eat a brog.'
jokes.setup: Jim asked Dwight to write his top 40 ideas; Dwight submitted 400, unable to cut them
jokes.punchline: The ideas escalate from 'eat a frog' (bad) to 'eat a dog' (worse and lazier) to 'eat a brog' (apparently a made-up portmanteau of frog and dog, which Dwight can't explain)
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'eat a frog' to 'eat a dog' to 'eat a brog' is a masterclass in comedic escalation — each step degrades the quality and logic of the prank while Dwight apparently couldn't see any of them as cuttable from his top 40. The invention of 'brog' (unexplained, apparently a portmanteau) and 'maybe I didn't understand it' is the perfect capstone. Dwight's absolute confidence in terrible ideas is the joke. Highly quotable ('eat a brog' in particular), strong rewatch bonus. Justifies 7.9 craft.

jokes.text: Andy deliberately infecting Erin's new computer with viruses: 'Allow all cookies? Why, soitenly. Pop-ups? Yes, please. Bit torrent streaming from a Somalian music website? Yeah, why not? I hope you don't get sick, Mr. Computer.'
jokes.setup: Andy has been given a used computer and is furious; he finds Erin's new computer unattended
jokes.punchline: Andy systematically destroying a computer while narrating his choices in the most deranged, polite voice — culminating in 'I hope you don't get sick, Mr. Computer'
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly unhinged Andy moment. The Three Stooges 'soitenly' is perfectly unexpected, the escalation from cookies to Somalian torrent sites is structured well, and 'I hope you don't get sick, Mr. Computer' — immediately after infecting it — is a beautiful piece of dark irony. This scene shows Andy's entitled rage filtered through his inability to be genuinely threatening. The 'Why are you doing this to me, Andy?' that follows makes the audience feel for the inanimate computer.

jokes.text: 'Why are you doing this to me, Andy?' — the computer seemingly 'responds' to Andy's sabotage (implicitly another character or Erin sees him)
jokes.setup: Andy is caught in the act of deliberately infecting the computer
jokes.punchline: The line 'Why are you doing this to me, Andy?' — whether said to him or in his head — frames Andy as personally victimizing a computer
jokes.explanation: A decent tag to the Andy computer bit. Works as a callback that gives the scene a button, but it's the weakest element of that sequence.

jokes.text: 'Because I hate your broke ass. And a 76ers fan to boot.'
jokes.setup: Andy explains why he's sabotaging the computer
jokes.punchline: His petty grievances escalate from the computer being 'broke' to its sports allegiances — a completely absurd reason to hate an inanimate object
jokes.explanation: The 76ers detail is a perfect absurdist escalation — Andy has anthropomorphized the computer to the point of hating its sports teams. The brevity and delivery are key. Good economy.

jokes.text: Packer tells Michael that Holly is laughing at complaints about him — 'She was laughing hysterically the whole time'
jokes.setup: Michael gently tells Packer that Holly mentioned some complaints about his behavior
jokes.punchline: Packer reframes it as Holly finding him hilarious — 'laughing hysterically the whole time' — which Michael immediately accepts as exoneration
jokes.explanation: Packer's spin on the complaints is predictable but fits his manipulative character. The joke is in Michael's credulous acceptance rather than Packer's reframe. Functional but not especially crafted.

jokes.text: Packer calls Holly's boyfriend uptight, suggests having Michael come to Florida to meet 'the local talent' — not realizing he's being sent to Florida as a trick
jokes.setup: Packer is excited about his new job and offers to include Michael in Florida adventures
jokes.punchline: The audience knows Packer is being tricked into going to Florida and won't have a cushy new job; his oblivious excitement is the dramatic irony
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is entirely situational — dramatic irony where the audience knows what Packer doesn't. Works because Packer's confidence and obliviousness are at peak levels right before his fall.

jokes.text: 'You've been on the road too long. You've been an outdoor cat. And now you have to be an indoor cat, so you can't be peeing all over the walls.'
jokes.setup: Michael is giving Packer sincere advice about adjusting to office life
jokes.punchline: Michael's metaphor: Packer is an outdoor cat who has been peeing on walls, who must now become an indoor cat
jokes.explanation: Michael's cat metaphor is both sincere and bizarre — he's genuinely trying to mentor Packer but can only reach for an analogy involving animals urinating on walls. The specificity of 'peeing all over the walls' as the defining outdoor-cat behavior, applied to a human's professional conduct, is very Michael. High character integration.

jokes.text: Packer: 'Michael, can I open the kimono with you?' Michael: (reaction)
jokes.setup: Packer wants to have a sincere conversation with Michael
jokes.punchline: Choosing 'open the kimono' — a business jargon phrase that sounds much more suggestive than intended, especially coming from Packer
jokes.explanation: A language joke that works because of the speaker — 'open the kimono' is a real business phrase but sounds wildly inappropriate when Packer says it. Functional but not particularly crafted.

jokes.text: Kevin's confessional: 'I should be apologizing to Packer, because everybody knows that I can dish it as good as I can take it.'
jokes.setup: Kevin has been told he doesn't have to accept Packer's apology
jokes.punchline: Kevin completely misreads the situation and tries to apologize to his bully, convinced he's the one who can take a joke
jokes.explanation: Kevin's complete misread of social dynamics — trying to apologize to his own bully because he believes himself to be a good sport — is both sad and funny. The earnestness of 'I can dish it as good as I can take it' from someone who clearly can't is a good character joke.

jokes.text: Packer's apology: 'I'm sorry if you were offended by my comments earlier.' Kevin: 'I wasn't offended.' Packer: 'Well, like I said...'
jokes.setup: Packer is forced to apologize to Kevin; the staff has gathered expecting a genuine apology
jokes.punchline: Packer's non-apology 'I'm sorry if you were offended' combined with Kevin's complete lack of offense and Packer's 'well, like I said' — the apology has no target
jokes.explanation: The textbook non-apology ('sorry if you were offended') is well-observed — it's precisely how insincere public apologies work. Ryan calling it 'textbook' and 'so un-cool' adds meta-commentary. Kevin's oblivious non-offense makes the whole ceremony pointless from both ends, which is the structural joke.

jokes.text: Packer's 'real' apology: 'Kevin, I am so sorry. You are skinny, and you're a genius.' — wildly overcorrecting
jokes.setup: The office demands a more genuine apology than Packer's non-apology
jokes.punchline: Packer swings to the opposite extreme: 'You are skinny and you're a genius' — transparently absurd flattery that is almost more insulting than the original comments
jokes.explanation: The overcorrection to 'skinny' and 'genius' is perfectly calibrated absurdist escalation — Packer goes from the minimum possible apology to the maximum possible lie. The specific choice of 'skinny' (the most false thing he could say about Kevin) makes it funnier than a generic compliment. Michael's 'okay, that was maybe too much' is the perfect acknowledgment that even Michael sees this as overreach.

jokes.text: Michael's 'apology' speech reveals Packer's backstory: 'Packer is a survivor of divorce, Stanley. Packer doesn't speak with his child, Meredith. Packer never lived up to his parents' expectations, Andy.'
jokes.setup: Michael tries to get people to empathize with Packer by listing his hardships
jokes.punchline: Each tragic detail is addressed to a specific coworker, but the details are too specifically sad — Michael is inadvertently just listing Packer's failures in front of everyone
jokes.explanation: Michael trying to generate sympathy by listing someone's failures is a great irony — he doesn't realize he's doing a roast instead of a defense. Addressing each failure to a specific person who shares that trait is an inspired structural choice.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Angela loves pussycats. Packer loves...' Packer: 'No, don't.' Michael: 'I was going to say dogs!'
jokes.setup: Michael is continuing his themed character comparisons; everyone (including Packer) assumes Michael is about to say something sexual
jokes.punchline: Michael claims he was going to say 'dogs' — but the audience and Packer both assumed something worse, and his protest may or may not be genuine
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly ambiguous joke. Michael — who uses 'that's what she said' for everything — may genuinely have meant 'dogs,' which makes the audience's assumption the joke. Or he's lying, which is also funny. The ambiguity is the craft. Packer panicking and Michael's wounded 'I was going to say dogs!' is a perfect comedic beat. The 'Angela loves pussycats' setup with 'pussycats' being both innocent and not is the structural foundation.

jokes.text: Jim and Dwight scheme to make the company laptop look used/old so Packer will be sent to Florida without realizing it's a trick; Dwight: 'We should break this hinge maybe.' Jim: 'Let's not go crazy.'
jokes.setup: Jim and Dwight are aging a new laptop to give to Packer as part of the Florida scheme
jokes.punchline: Jim — who just suggested breaking the computer — tells Dwight 'let's not go crazy' when Dwight wants to break the hinge
jokes.explanation: A functional irony beat — Jim drawing an arbitrary line while already doing something questionable. Dwight and Jim collaborating on pranks is always fun, and Jim's 'let's not go crazy' is character-appropriate while being situationally absurd.

jokes.text: Dwight's cover story for the laptop: 'An elegant old lady kept it around in case her grandkids came to visit. But they died, and they never came.' Dwight: 'I'm gonna make myself cry.'
jokes.setup: Jim and Dwight are fabricating a backstory for the old laptop
jokes.punchline: Dwight goes full dark novelist — the grandkids are dead, they never came — and then becomes emotionally invested in his own invented tragedy
jokes.explanation: An outstanding Dwight character moment. The unnecessary specificity of the dead grandchildren, combined with Dwight's emotional immersion in a story he just invented 10 seconds ago, is quintessential Dwight. 'I'm gonna make myself cry' is the perfect button — he's moved by his own fabrication. This is the kind of joke that showcases how well the writers understand Dwight's specific brand of earnest darkness.

jokes.text: Michael's elaborate misdirection: sending Packer to 'Jo's place in Florida,' telling him to hop a locked gate, check out Harry Potter World — an entirely fake cushy job setup
jokes.setup: Michael is orchestrating Packer's removal by tricking him into thinking he got a great new corporate job in Florida
jokes.punchline: The scheme is absurdly elaborate and loving — Michael is putting real effort into making Florida sound appealing even though he's essentially firing his best friend
jokes.explanation: The comedy is situational — Michael going to ridiculous lengths to be kind while also getting rid of someone. 'I'm a huge alligator nerd' from Packer is a good line. Functional but not the strongest joke construction.

jokes.text: Packer: 'Also, I'm a huge boob nerd.'
jokes.setup: Packer is explaining his interests and mentions being an alligator nerd
jokes.punchline: 'Also, I'm a huge boob nerd' — a non-sequitur added with perfect casual equivalence to alligator expertise
jokes.explanation: A quick Packer character beat that works because of the structure — it rides the 'nerd' framing and pivots to something completely base. Economy is excellent. Not a crafted joke so much as a perfect character sentence.

jokes.text: Holly to Michael after Packer leaves: 'I'm sorry about your friend.' Michael: 'No. He's an ass.' Holly: 'You are.' Michael: 'What are you, wicked smaht?'
jokes.setup: Holly tries to comfort Michael with the implication that he handled a hard situation with a friend; Michael deflects
jokes.punchline: Holly turns it back on Michael ('You are' — calling him an ass for the scheme); Michael deflects with a Boston accent 'wicked smaht' — a Good Will Hunting reference
jokes.explanation: A sweet-funny moment for Michael/Holly. Holly calling Michael an ass (deservedly) and Michael deflecting with 'wicked smaht' is charming — it shows their chemistry. The Good Will Hunting reference is slightly dated but works as a Michael character choice.

jokes.text: Darryl discovers Pam found Andy's computer 'in the warehouse.' Darryl: 'I know every inch of that warehouse... Maybe you could go back down there and find me some extra sick days.'
jokes.setup: Pam says she found the computer in the warehouse; Darryl points out he knows every inch of the warehouse and didn't 'find' it
jokes.punchline: Darryl pivots from calling out the lie to immediately asking for sick days — aligning himself with the corruption rather than reporting it
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best final beats. Darryl effortlessly transitions from calling out Pam's lie to immediately leveraging it for personal gain — 'maybe you could find me some extra sick days' — without a moment of moral deliberation. It's in perfect character for Darryl, efficiently executed, and deeply quotable. The confidence of the pivot is what makes it exceptional.

jokes.text: Pam and Darryl negotiating sick days: 'I think I saw one sick day.' 'I think maybe I saw five.' 'Three.' Pam's talking head: 'I'm full-on corrupt.'
jokes.setup: Darryl has leverage on Pam; she negotiates a sick-day bribe with him
jokes.punchline: The absurd casualness of the negotiation ('one... five... three') followed by Pam's confessional confession: 'I'm full-on corrupt'
jokes.explanation: A fantastic ending. The negotiation is structured like a real back-room deal with Pam as the briber. 'I'm full-on corrupt' in Pam's confessional is a perfect button — she's not even that bothered, which is the joke. The Pam character journey from season 1 (meek receptionist) to this moment is part of what makes the line land. Highly quotable. Great callback/escalation from the warehouse catch.

tmdb_overview: Traveling salesman Todd Packer comes to Dunder Mifflin looking for a desk job in the office. However, the office is unsure if they want him to work there due to his previous behavior. After dealing with computer problems, Andy confronts office administrator Pam to get a new computer.
